content: 1. Three hospital-based cross-sectional surveys were conducted, alongside one community-based cohort study, one cross-sectional survey with qualitative components, one household-level cross-sectional survey, one retrospective hospital-based cohort study, one cohort analytic study, one before-and-after study with qualitative components, and one study utilizing data from the vital registration system. 2. Six studies included three pre-and-post intervention studies, one of which incorporated mixed methods, one interrupted time series analysis, one retrospective pre-and-post analysis, and one longitudinal panel survey. 3. The quality of evidence was assessed across studies and categorized as high, moderate, low, or very low. Variability in values and preferences was also evaluated, with greater variability or uncertainty warranting conditional recommendations. 4. WHO recommendations on health promotion interventions for maternal and newborn health included 70 interventions, such as birth preparedness and complication readiness (BPCR), male involvement interventions, promotion of human rights awareness, maternity waiting homes (MWHs), community-organized transport schemes, and new roles for traditional birth attendants (TBAs). 5. The balance of benefits versus harms was analyzed, with outcomes categorized as benefits outweighing harms, benefits and harms being balanced, or harms outweighing benefits. The larger the difference between benefits and harms, the more likely a strong recommendation was warranted. 6. Resource use was evaluated as less resource-intensive, more resource-intensive, or unable to determine. Strong recommendations were made when benefits clearly outweighed harms and resource use was justified. 7. A variety of study designs were employed, including randomized controlled trials (RCTs), cluster RCTs, quasi-experimental studies, controlled before-and-after studies, one-group before-and-after evaluations, pre-and-post comparative studies with or without controls, and retrospective analyses. 8. In Tanzania (2003), rural interventions included house visits by volunteers to provide BPCR education to pregnant women and their families, community surveillance systems for pregnancies, and community-based transport plans using methods such as canoes, ox carts, bicycles, and stretchers. 9. In Eritrea (2008), maternity waiting homes were established in remote areas, providing consumables and ambulance services for referrals. Cultural adaptation of maternity care services was emphasized. 10. In Pakistan (2011), a community-based intervention package was delivered through lady health workers and community health committees (CHCs), which organized emergency transport funds and utilized local resources for vehicles. 11. In Uganda (2009), community perceptions of health facilities were summarized into report cards and presented during community meetings. Action plans were developed collaboratively with community members and health staff. 12. In Zimbabwe (1994), free self-catering temporary accommodations were provided 150 meters from labor wards for high-risk women identified during antenatal care (ANC). MWHs offered ANC and health education. 13. In Bangladesh (2010), antenatal house visits by volunteers promoted BPCR and newborn education. Community health workers conducted postnatal visits to promote preventive newborn care practices and refer sick neonates. 14. In Kenya (2007), a quasi-experimental pre-and-post study involved behavior change campaigns using printed materials, drama, and meetings. Facility upgrades and provider skill improvements were also implemented. 15. In Tanzania (2007), participatory village-level meetings and theater performances were used to mobilize communities. Maternity care quality was improved through infrastructure strengthening and provider training. 16. In Bangladesh (1991), nurse-midwives were posted in rural outposts to work with community health workers and TBAs, ensuring their presence during labor. 17. In Guatemala (2004), service delivery improvements and behavior change interventions were implemented to organize communities for obstetric emergencies. A community action cycle was introduced, including steps such as dialogue, planning, and participatory evaluation. 18. In Indonesia (2009), a village midwife program trained and placed midwives in poor, remote communities. Community mobilization efforts aimed to reduce delays in transporting women and newborns for complications and increase family planning use. 19. In Peru (2009), a culturally appropriate childbirth care model was developed with Quechua communities and health professionals. Social mobilization campaigns and community health committees addressed health concerns. 20. In Ethiopia (2010), a 40-bed MWH was established within hospital grounds for high-risk women to spend the last weeks of pregnancy. Mixed-method approaches, including audits and hospital database reviews, were used to evaluate outcomes. 21. In Australia (2012), the Murrie Clinic provided antenatal services to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women, including transportation and home visits. 22. In India (2012), a rural intervention package included home visits, community meetings, folk-song sessions, and stakeholder meetings. Control clusters received standard care. 23. In South Africa (1978), MWHs were established for high-risk women in rural areas. 24. In Malawi (2001), villages were equipped with bicycle ambulances to improve emergency transport for maternal care. 25. In China (2012), the Gender and Health Equity Network (GHEN) supported local health planning for women’s health and increased women’s participation in health planning. Efforts were made to improve prevention and care at the household level. 26. In the USA (2000), minority health coalitions developed projects to increase access to early ANC for minority women through community outreach and addressing cultural barriers. 27. Across studies, interventions often included community mobilization, participatory approaches, and stakeholder engagement to improve maternal and newborn health outcomes.
